t: In the narrow sense, the Iberians were the pre-Indo-European peoples of the eastern and southern coasts of the peninsula that bears their name, distinct from the Celts and Celtiberians of its interior.
From the late 5th century BCE their societies centred on fortified towns, oppida, led by aristocracies and by chieftains bound to their followers by a tie the Romans called fides.
Iberian soldiers fought in Italy, Greece and Sicily and for both sides in the Second Punic War, after which their lands became Roman provinces and their language gave way to Latin.
dyk: According to Arrian, the Iberians sent envoys to Alexander the Great in 324 BCE, along with embassies of Carthaginians, Italics and Gauls, to ask for his friendship.
ev: Greek colonists make the first historical reference to the Iberians, as the non-Celtic peoples south of the Ebro
A great fortress is built at Saguntum, and Iberian soldiers begin to fight in Italy, Greece and Sicily
An aristocracy and a system of clients take hold, and the oppidum becomes the centre of political life
Iberian envoys seek the friendship of Alexander the Great
Hannibal takes command of the Carthaginian forces and completes the conquest of the Iberians south of the Ebro
Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus arrives in Iberia and turns the war against Carthage
The Iberian tribes of Hispania Citerior revolt against Rome
The Iberian language dies out, replaced by Latin

f.homeland: The eastern and southern coasts of the Iberian Peninsula: today’s Catalonia, eastern and northern Aragon, the Valencian Community, the Region of Murcia, eastern Andalusia and perhaps the Balearic Islands, with Roussillon and parts of Languedoc in France; key sites Castellet de Banyoles at Tivissa, Ullastret, Saguntum, Lucentum, Pozo Moro, Baza, Elche
f.period: Iberian culture from the 6th century BCE, perhaps with far older roots; the Iberian language spoken from the 7th to at least the 1st century BCE; an aristocracy and oppida from the late 5th and early 4th centuries BCE; Carthaginian conquest south of the Ebro under the Barcids, then Roman conquest during and after the Second Punic War; the language extinct by the 1st to 2nd centuries CE
f.known: oppida and chieftains bound to followers by fides; sculpture such as the Lady of Elche and the Lady of Baza; pottery painted with red geometric designs; the falcata and other iron weapons; soldiers and cavalry serving Carthage and Rome; the Iberian semi-syllabic scripts
f.sources: Greek and Roman writers from Hecataeus of Miletus and Herodotus to Strabo, Avienius, Arrian and Silius Italicus; excavations of settlements, sanctuaries and tombs; Iberian inscriptions in three scripts, in a language still unclassified
